subsection: 12. Religion, the mass media and mass higher education in modern American culture

notes.h: The setting: Cold War, prosperity and the First Amendment
notes.b: Three background facts explain why religion became so public after 1945. The Cold War made faith a political weapon, new wealth moved families to the suburbs, and the Constitution set rules on how far government could support religion.
points: The Cold War was the long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, an atheist state, so Americans could present their own religious faith as a mark of difference from their enemy.
The red scare was the fear of communist spies and influence at home, which made public displays of faith and patriotism seem like proof of loyalty.
Post-war prosperity and the baby boom (the sharp rise in births after 1945) sent young families to new suburbs, where they needed churches, schools and community life.

The First Amendment forbids Congress from establishing a religion, and the Supreme Court read this as a separation of church and state, which is why prayer in public schools later became a legal battleground.
notes.tip: Examiners reward dated evidence, so tie each background factor to a later event: anti-communism to the Pledge in 1954, suburbs to church building, the First Amendment to the school prayer rulings of 1962-63.

notes.h: The post-war religious revival
notes.b: Church membership and religious observance grew strongly in the 1950s. Prosperity, the suburbs and the Cold War all pushed Americans towards their churches.
points: Church membership rose from about half of Americans around 1940 to about two-thirds by 1960, so the 1950s are often called a religious revival.

New churches were built in the suburbs in large numbers, and church groups and social clubs became central to suburban community life, because newcomers used the church to make friends and find a place in a new neighbourhood.
Norman Vincent Peale's The Power of Positive Thinking (1952) was a best seller that mixed religion with self-help, showing how faith was sold as a way to personal success and calm.
The rise of the megachurch (a very large congregation) and of television ministry followed, building on this appetite for popular religion.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph on the revival, cover church membership, the Pledge (1954), the motto (1956), anti-communism and suburban churches, each with its date or figure.

notes.h: Civil religion and the Cold War
notes.b: Civil religion means a shared public faith in the nation under God, expressed by the government rather than by any one church. In the 1950s it was used to set the United States against atheistic communism.
points: Congress added the words under God to the Pledge of Allegiance on 14 June 1954, and a law of July 1956 made In God We Trust the national motto.
The Cold War gave religion a political role: communism was condemned as atheistic, so the Pledge and motto changes were part of the struggle against it.
Many commentators saw religion as a bulwark (a defensive wall) against communism, and presidents from Eisenhower onwards attended church and spoke of the nation's faith.
Eisenhower was baptised in February 1953, soon after taking office, and he said in 1952 that government made no sense without a deeply felt religious faith, and that it did not matter which faith.
That remark is often quoted as an example of the civil religion of the period, because it valued faith itself above any particular church.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two dates: under God in the Pledge is 1954, In God We Trust as the motto is 1956.

notes.h: Black churches and the civil rights movement
notes.b: For Black Americans in the South the church was one of the few institutions they controlled themselves. This made it the natural base for the struggle against segregation.
points: Black churches, such as the Baptist congregations of the South, provided the meeting places, leadership and fundraising networks on which the civil rights movement depended.
The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-56 was organised from Black churches and led by Martin Luther King, a Baptist minister, which shows how a congregation could be turned into a protest organisation.
The Southern Christian Leadership Conference (1957) was led by ministers, so the movement's leaders spoke in religious language that Americans of all races knew.
notes.tip: Here you only need Black churches as an institution: meeting places, leaders and funds, with Montgomery as your example.

notes.h: Key personality: Billy Graham
notes.b: Billy Graham was the best-known preacher of the revival and a participant in it. He used radio, the press and mass rallies to reach millions, and he became close to presidents.
points: William Franklin Graham was born on 7 November 1918 near Charlotte, North Carolina, studied at Wheaton College in Illinois and was ordained a Southern Baptist minister. He died in 2018.

His Los Angeles crusade (a series of mass evangelistic meetings) of September to November 1949 was planned for three weeks but extended to eight after wide press coverage, helped by the Hearst newspapers, and it made him a national figure.
He founded the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association in 1950 and began a radio programme, Hour of Decision, which later reached a worldwide audience, so his message travelled far beyond the stadiums.
He co-founded the magazine Christianity Today in 1956, edited by Carl Henry, to give a conservative evangelical voice alongside the mainstream press.

He held crusades at Harringay Arena in London in 1954 and at Madison Square Garden in New York in 1957, which ran for about sixteen weeks, and he later spoke at large stadium rallies across the world.
He took his message into the Cold War divide with a visit to Moscow in 1982, and he organised the Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization in 1974, which made him a leader of world evangelicalism.
Radio, television and mass rallies were his tools, and the Cold War gave his preaching extra force, because Americans were ready to hear faith set against atheistic communism.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on Graham, give birth and training, the 1949 Los Angeles crusade and why it succeeded (press coverage), the Association and radio in 1950, Christianity Today in 1956, then the crusades and presidents. Each dated fact earns marks.

notes.h: Key personality: Billy Graham, presidents, race and judgements
notes.b: Graham's closeness to power shaped his career, and events in turn changed how he used it. Contemporaries and historians have both been divided about his legacy.
points: He became a regular adviser and visitor to presidents from Eisenhower onwards and preached at presidential events, which brought him close to the centre of political life.

His link with Truman began awkwardly in 1950, when he was criticised for revealing his talk with the president, but he became a friend and adviser of Eisenhower and Nixon, and he supported Nixon in 1960 and 1968.

Watergate damaged his standing: he said afterwards that he had been used and that he would keep out of partisan politics, and he kept his distance from Falwell's Moral Majority and warned against mixing religion with party politics.
From the Chattanooga crusade of 1953 he had the ropes dividing white and Black seating taken down, an early sign of his commitment to racial integration.
King prayed at Graham's New York crusade of 1957, but Graham did not endorse the mass protests of the early 1960s and urged patience, so he was criticised for not supporting King more openly.
Contemporaries were divided: admirers saw him as a unifying figure who spoke to millions, while liberal theologians and other critics saw him as a tool of Cold War patriotism.
Historians judge his influence on modern evangelicalism as very large, but note that his closeness to presidents, and above all to Nixon, compromised his independence.
Tapes of a 1972 conversation with Nixon, released in 2002, caught Graham making anti-Semitic remarks, for which he apologised.
notes.tip: A top answer names a limit as well as achievements: his closeness to Nixon and his caution on civil rights. Remember that Graham avoided party politics after Watergate, while Falwell was openly partisan.

notes.h: Catholic America and the 1960 election
notes.b: Catholics were a large minority, and many Protestants doubted that a Catholic could be loyal to the president's office rather than to the Pope. The election of John F. Kennedy in 1960 tested that fear and weakened it.
points: Al Smith, a Catholic Democrat, was defeated in the presidential election of 1928 amid anti-Catholic prejudice, so Kennedy knew that his faith could cost him votes.
In 1960 some Protestant ministers, including Norman Vincent Peale, questioned the idea of a Catholic president, fearing he would take orders from the Pope.
Kennedy answered at the Greater Houston Ministerial Association on 12 September 1960, saying that he believed in an America where the separation of church and state was absolute.
He beat Nixon narrowly in November 1960 with strong support from Catholic voters and became the first Catholic president, which weakened the old Protestant dominance of national politics.
Catholic life in the 1950s was strong, with parish schools, church building and Bishop Fulton Sheen, whose television series Life Is Worth Living ran from 1952 to 1957 and reached millions.
Will Herberg's Protestant, Catholic, Jew (1955) popularised the view that Catholics and Jews, as well as Protestants, were part of a common American religious tradition.
notes.tip: Give the Houston speech as a point about the separation of church and state, and link it to Al Smith's defeat in 1928 to show how much had changed.

notes.h: Fundamentalism, evangelicalism and the religious right
notes.b: Three terms are easily confused. Fundamentalism and evangelicalism are kinds of conservative Protestant belief, while the religious right is a political movement that grew out of them.
points: Fundamentalism rejects modernist readings of the Bible (readings that fit scripture to modern science) and holds to the literal truth of scripture, and it is usually separatist, keeping apart from other churches.
Fundamentalism is traced to the early twentieth century and the 1925 Scopes trial in Tennessee, which was about a teacher accused of teaching evolution.
Evangelicalism is wider: it stresses personal conversion (a believer's own turning to Christ) and evangelism (spreading the faith), so it takes in more churches than fundamentalism does.
The National Association of Evangelicals, founded in 1942, brought together a broad group of conservative churches under this evangelical banner.
notes.tip: Short questions ask you to define fundamentalism in one or two precise sentences: literal truth of the Bible and rejection of modernist readings.

notes.h: School prayer rulings and the conservative backlash
notes.b: In the early 1960s the Supreme Court applied the separation of church and state to public schools. Many religious conservatives saw this as an attack on faith, and it helped them become a political force.
points: In Engel v Vitale (1962) the Supreme Court ruled that state-written school prayer was unconstitutional, a decision that provoked strong protest from religious conservatives.
In Abington School District v Schempp (1963) the Court ruled that compulsory Bible reading in public schools was unconstitutional.
These two decisions helped to mobilise conservative Christians, because they felt that religion was being pushed out of public life.
notes.tip: Keep the two cases apart: Engel v Vitale is prayer (1962), Schempp is Bible reading (1963). Dated evidence from 1962-63 is rewarded in the 100-mark essay.

notes.h: Televangelism
notes.b: Televangelists are preachers who use television to reach a mass audience. Programmes could reach far more people than any church building, so television became a way to raise money and shape politics.
points: Jerry Falwell, a Baptist pastor from Lynchburg, Virginia, reached a national audience with his Old Time Gospel Hour from the 1970s.
Pat Robertson founded the Christian Broadcasting Network, and its programme The 700 Club began in 1966.
Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker built the PTL ministry, and televangelists such as these used broadcasts to raise money and to influence politics.
Televangelists reached audiences far larger than most local churches could, and their programmes often combined religious teaching with political messages.
The Bakker scandal of 1987 involved the misuse of funds and a sex scandal, and Jim Bakker was later convicted of fraud and jailed, which damaged the reputation of televangelism.
Jimmy Swaggart's scandal of 1988 added to the damage, so by the end of the decade the image of televangelism had suffered badly.
notes.tip: Describe televangelism through its audience, fundraising and political messages, and date the scandals 1987-88.

notes.h: Issues of the 1970s and the evangelicals
notes.b: In the 1970s new social questions gave conservative Christians fresh reasons to organise. Their relationship with the White House also changed.
points: Roe v Wade (1973) on abortion, and the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), passed by Congress in 1972 and opposed by conservative Christians led by Phyllis Schlafly, became issues that mobilised the religious right.
In 1977 the singer Anita Bryant campaigned against a gay rights ordinance in Dade County, Florida, which gave conservative Christians another cause.
Jimmy Carter, a born-again Southern Baptist, was elected in 1976, and the press called 1976 the year of the evangelical.
Many evangelicals turned against Carter by 1980, over abortion and the Equal Rights Amendment, which left them looking for a different leader.
notes.tip: Mention Roe v Wade and the ERA only as issues that mobilised conservative Christians.

notes.h: The Moral Majority and the religious right
notes.b: From 1979 conservative Christians became an organised political force, closely associated with the Republican Party and Ronald Reagan. The Moral Majority was the organisation that brought them together.
points: The Moral Majority was founded in 1979 by Jerry Falwell with conservative organisers such as Paul Weyrich, and it campaigned against abortion, the ERA, gay rights and pornography, and for school prayer and a strong defence.
It used direct-mail lists (letters sent to supporters) to raise funds and register voters, and it mobilised conservative churches and voters before the 1980 election.

Its support helped the Republican campaign of Ronald Reagan: in August 1980 he told a conference of conservative Christians in Dallas that he knew they could not endorse him but that he endorsed them.
The Republican platform of 1980 opposed abortion and backed school prayer, which rewarded the movement's voters.
Critics saw the movement as a threat to the separation of church and state.
Its influence was greatest in the early 1980s, and it declined after its leaders were embarrassed by the scandals of the late 1980s and the failure of its political strategy.

Falwell wound up the Moral Majority in 1989, but its voters and organisers moved into groups such as Robertson's Christian Coalition, founded in 1989, so the religious right remained part of the Republican coalition.
notes.tip: Exams ask who founded it and when, its aims, its role in 1980 and why it faded. Define it as the 1979 organisation of the religious right founded by Jerry Falwell.

notes.h: Mass media: television, news and public opinion
notes.b: The mass media are the means of reaching most homes at once: television, radio, the press and magazines. In the 1950s and 1960s television became the strongest of them, and it shaped public opinion, meaning the views of ordinary Americans as measured by polls and influenced by what they saw.
points: Television spread through American homes in the 1950s, and most homes had a set by 1960, so network news became the principal source of national news for millions.
CBS (2 September 1963) and NBC (9 September 1963) lengthened their evening news to thirty minutes, and opinion surveys from the early 1960s found television the main news source for most Americans.
The first televised presidential debate, between Kennedy and Nixon in Chicago on 26 September 1960, was watched by a large audience and is widely credited with shaping the outcome of the election.
The quiz show scandal of 1958 showed that contestants on shows such as Twenty-One had been given answers, and Charles Van Doren was among them, so public trust in television suffered.
Congressional hearings followed in 1959, and a law of 1960 banned the rigging of quiz shows.
notes.tip: Always link the medium to a political effect, not just describe it: the debate helped decide the 1960 election, and the quiz scandal damaged trust in television.

notes.h: News and Vietnam: the first television war
notes.b: Vietnam was the first war that Americans watched in their living rooms. Historians still debate how far the pictures changed public opinion, but the coverage clearly showed the power of television news.
points: Morley Safer of CBS filmed Marines burning the village of Cam Ne in August 1965, and the report showed viewers a side of the war that official briefings did not.
During the Tet Offensive of January and February 1968 the Eddie Adams photograph of a Viet Cong prisoner being shot in Saigon became one of the images that shaped opinion.
Walter Cronkite's report of 27 February 1968 saw the war as a stalemate, and it was one report among several that influenced public opinion.
The photograph by Nick Ut of a child burned by napalm, in June 1972, was another image that turned opinion against the war.
The debate is over cause and effect: the media may have shaped opinion, but opinion also shaped what viewers wanted to see and what governments could do.
notes.tip: Do not say that Cronkite's broadcast caused Johnson's decision not to stand again, as the evidence is weak. Say it was one report among several that influenced opinion.

notes.h: The press, Watergate and the check on government
notes.b: In the early 1970s the press and television showed that they could expose wrongdoing at the top of government. This strengthened their role as a check on power.
points: The Pentagon Papers, a secret government study of the Vietnam War, were published in June 1971 by the New York Times and the Washington Post, and they revealed government deception.
After the Watergate break-in of 17 June 1972, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein of the Washington Post reported the burglary and the cover-up, which showed the press's power to expose a presidency.
The Senate Watergate hearings of 1973 were televised live, so the public watched the evidence for themselves.
The revelation of the White House tapes made the media a central actor in the downfall of Nixon, who resigned on 9 August 1974.
notes.tip: Here you need only the role of the press and the media, with the dates 1971, 1972, 1973 and 1974. Do not confuse the Kennedy-Nixon debate (1960) with the Senate Watergate hearings (1973).

notes.h: Public broadcasting, advertising and later developments
notes.b: Alongside news, the media sold goods and made celebrities. Government and business also changed the shape of broadcasting.
points: The Public Broadcasting Act of 1967 created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, and the Public Broadcasting Service, the public television network, began broadcasting in 1970.
Advertising expanded rapidly on television and in magazines, so the mass media turned consumer goods and celebrity into central features of public life.

The FCC (the Federal Communications Commission, which regulates broadcasting) abolished the Fairness Doctrine in 1987. This rule had required stations to give time to opposing views, so its end helped talk radio and partisan broadcasting to grow.
Cable television expanded with CNN in 1980 and MTV in 1981.
notes.tip: Say what the Fairness Doctrine was before you say what its abolition caused.

notes.h: Mass higher education
notes.b: Before 1945 a college degree was for a small minority. After the war government money and a growing population opened the colleges to millions.
points: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act, known as the GI Bill, of June 1944 paid for veterans to study, and about two million veterans attended college under it by the mid-1950s, many of them the first in their families to do so.
College enrolment roughly tripled between about 1950 and 1970, from under three million to about eight million, helped by affluence and the baby boom.
The Sputnik shock of 1957 led to the National Defense Education Act of 1958, which gave more federal funding to universities, especially for science and languages.
The Higher Education Act of 1965 provided federal scholarships and loans, and extended federal support to students and institutions.
The California Master Plan for Higher Education of 1960 set out a three-tier system of the University of California, state colleges and community colleges, and became a model for other states.
The University of California's president Clark Kerr described the huge research university as a multiversity, which is a university with many purposes and a very large size.
notes.tip: To explain why numbers grew, give the GI Bill, affluence and federal aid. Keep the three laws apart: the GI Bill (1944, veterans), the NDEA (1958) and the Higher Education Act (1965, grants and loans).

notes.h: The Free Speech Movement at Berkeley
notes.b: In 1964 students at Berkeley, part of the University of California, fought for the right to organise politics on campus.
points: The movement began in September 1964 when the university banned political tables and recruiting on a strip of campus, so students protested against restrictions on political activity.
Berkeley's size and impersonality were among the grievances, because students felt treated as parts of a machine rather than as individuals.
Mario Savio's speech of 2 December 1964 urged students to put their bodies upon the gears of the machine, and the sit-in in Sproul Hall that followed became the movement's best-known protest.
About 800 students were arrested at Sproul Hall on 2 and 3 December 1964.
Soon after, students were allowed more freedom of political activity, as the rules on political activity were relaxed.
notes.tip: For the Free Speech Movement give cause, leader, protest and outcome: the ban, Savio, Sproul Hall and the arrests, then relaxed rules.

notes.h: Campus protest spreads
notes.b: After Berkeley, protest moved from campus rights to the war in Vietnam. Several campuses saw occupations and deaths.
points: Students occupied buildings at Columbia University in April 1968, and campus protest spread to many universities through the anti-war movement.
On 4 May 1970 the National Guard killed four students at Kent State University in Ohio, which brought mass student strikes across the country.
A few days later police killed two students at Jackson State College in Mississippi.
Hundreds of campuses went on strike after these shootings.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Kent State (4 May 1970, National Guard) with Jackson State (days later, police). Keep the Free Speech Movement (1964, campus rights) apart from the anti-war protests of 1965-70.

notes.h: Assessment: did religion, media and education shape public life?
notes.b: Examiners reward judgements that set achievements against limits, and contemporary views against later ones. Public opinion links all three areas, because the media shaped it and it in turn shaped policy.
points: Religion: supporters argue that faith gave Americans a common identity against communism and a moral basis for civil rights, as the Black churches showed.

Religion: critics argue that the religious right of the 1980s narrowed debate on social issues and politicised religion, and that televangelism, hit by the scandals of 1987-88, encouraged dependence on wealthy donors.
Media: television made politics more visible and personal, which helped Kennedy and Reagan, and it held governments to account over Vietnam and Watergate.
Media: critics point to commercialism, image over substance and the deception of the quiz show scandal.
Higher education: mass higher education gave many more Americans social mobility and opportunity.
Higher education: it also produced campus unrest and debates about the role of universities in politics and society.
Contemporaries and later historians differ: Graham's admirers saw a unifying figure, while later historians stress his closeness to Nixon.
notes.tip: In a judgement answer name a limit as well as an achievement, and use a dated example for each: 1954 and 1956, 1962-63, 1979-80.

keyTerms.definition: A conservative strand of Protestantism that holds to the literal truth of the Bible and rejects modernist interpretations of scripture.
The organised conservative Christian political movement founded in 1979 by Jerry Falwell, campaigning on abortion, the family and school issues.
Television, radio, newspapers and magazines, which by 1960 reached most American homes and shaped politics, war and culture.
The views of ordinary Americans, measured by polls and shaped by the media, which in this period influenced responses to religion, war and politics.
A Protestant movement stressing personal conversion, the authority of scripture and evangelism, represented by the National Association of Evangelicals.
The use of television broadcasts by preachers to reach large audiences, raise money and promote religious and political causes.
The student protest at the University of California, Berkeley, from September 1964, which defended political activity on campus.
The expansion of college and university places after 1945, supported by the GI Bill and federal aid, which made higher education available to far more Americans.
The shared public faith in America's God-given mission, expressed in the Pledge, the motto and presidential appeals to religion, which was strong in the 1950s.
The FCC rule requiring broadcasters to present contrasting views on controversial issues, abolished in 1987.
